articles.title: Paula Badosa gana en 10 minutos y no nota los 40 días de parón
articles.standfirst: La tenista nacida en Nueva York, verdugo de Kasatkina, se motiva especialmente en la ciudad de los rascacielos
articles.summary: La tenista nacida en Nueva York, verdugo de Kasatkina, se motiva especialmente en la ciudad de los rascacielos
articles.body: Paula Badosa nació en Nueva York el 15 de noviembre de 1997. Eso la convierte en un peligro en la ciudad de los rascacielos con independencia de su momento por su motivación extra para hacerlo bien. A pesar de los 40 días sin competir, tras una intervención que le privó de participar en la gira previa de torneos por Norteamérica, la catalana certificó este miércoles su pase a la segunda ronda del US Open tras apear a Daria Kasatkina, por 6-1 y 6-4. El duelo que debió terminar el martes, y se suspendió por la lluvia tras tres bolas de clasificación, acabó 24 horas después en apenas 10 minutos. Paula empata a cuatro victorias el cara a cara entre ambas. Para encontrar su último partido oficial había que remontarse al 24 de julio en Hamburgo. Badosa y Kasatkina personifican dos realidades totalmente diferentes. La ambición de la primera contrasta con la sensación de haberse dejado ir de Dasha, que triunfó en su día como rusa y que ahora pasa sin hacer ruido por la WTA como australiana. Cada uno de sus turnos de saque era una oportunidad de rotura para su rival, tanto por el porcentaje como la escasa velocidad. La pupila de Pol Toledo, una de las tenistas que más fuerte le pega, aceptaba todos los regalos. Se anotó la manga inicial cediendo un único juego. A la novena bola de triunfo fue la vencida para ella. Paula, de 28 años y la 87 de las listas, tiene en los cuartos de 2024 su mejor resultado en el Abierto estadounidense. Se ausentó de la pasada edición por lesión. El triunfo le vale 70 puntos, que son los mismos que sumó esta campaña en el Open de Australia. No jugó en Roland Garros y perdió a la primera en Wimbledon. Badosa espera en la segunda ronda a Coco Gauff. La estadounidense, cuarta cabeza de serie, viene de adjudicarse el WTA 1000 de Cincinnati. La campeona del US Open en su edición de 2023 es una de las cuatro jugadoras que aspira a salir del torneo neoyorquino con el número uno debajo del brazo. La española se agarra a sus 17 victorias ante rivales del 'top10', la última de ellas frente a Coco en los octavos del 500 de Berlín.

articles.body: Paula Badosa, después de apear a la australiana Daria Kasatkina en la primera ronda del US Open 2026, mira al futuro con optimismo a pesar de tener que enfrentarse este viernes con Coco Gauff. La estadounidense, cuarta del ranking y campeona del torneo hace apenas tres años, viene en forma como lo demuestra su reciente título en el WTA 1000 de Cincinnati. Badosa, sin embargo, no renuncia a dar la sorpresa. Con más a ganar que a perder, tras perderse toda la gira americana de pista dura a causa de una intervención, se agarra al hecho de que Coco se le da especialmente bien. Acumula 17 victorias por 22 derrotas ante adversarias del 'top10'. De los ocho precedentes entre ambas se ha anotado cinco. El último de ellos fue en los octavos del torneo de categoría 500 de Berlín. Gauff es una de las cuatro tenistas que pueden salir de Nueva York como números uno. Las otras tres son Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina y Jessica Pegula. articles.title: Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend win second-round US Open matches in warp speed
articles.summary: Americans Jessica Pegula and Taylor Townsend are among the first US Open players into the third round after quick wins on Wednesday, Sept. 2.
articles.body:
Day 4 of US Open singles draw play generated quick wins for American tennis stars Jessica Pegula and Taylor Townsend.

This is good news because rain has been an issue for the tournament, and players are still concluding first-round matches in an effort to catch up.

In the luck of the draw, Pegula and Townsend have not dealt with rain or weather-related issues. They needed 56 and 48 minutes, respectively, to secure their wins.

Pegula lost just four games, defeating fellow American Sofia Kenin, 6-3, 6-1.

August 31, 2026; New York, United States; Taylor Townsend of the U.S. in action during her first round match against Poland's Maja Chwalinska. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images

Townsend lost two games, and in an amazing stat, won every one of her first serve points (23-for-23) in her 6-1, 6-1 win over Australian Taylah Preston.

Besides advancing in singles, Townsend, 30, will play women's doubles with longtime partner Katerina Siniakova. The duo is the top-seeded team in a US Open draw that also includes Venus and Serena Williams.

The US Open is the only Grand Slam Townsend has never won in doubles. She won Wimbledon in 2024, the Australian Open in 2025 and the 2026 French Open, all with Siniakova.

It's early in the tournament, and there is a lot of tennis to be played, but Pegula and Townsend are proving they are names to watch as the US Open moves into the latter rounds.

Watch the US Open on ESPN through Sept. 13.

articles.title: “Distracting The Actual Player”: Influencers Called Out For US Open Behavior By Sports Broadcaster
articles.summary: With the game locked at deuce in the second set of the fourth game of her first-round match at the 2026 US Open, Naomi Osaka had to hold her serve upon an in...
articles.body:
With the game locked at deuce in the second set of the fourth game of her first-round match at the 2026 US Open, Naomi Osaka had to hold her serve upon an instruction from the umpire. You would think that having to stop the action at such a crucial stage of the game was because of an injury or a controversial call. But that was not the case. The umpire had to put the game on hold to address some attendees who appeared to be influencers and had begun staging a proper photoshoot session in a way that seemed to be distracting the players.

As expected, the incident has gone on to spark plenty of backlash and criticism from tennis fans. Influencer and sports broadcaster Emily Austin also weighed in on the situation, sharing her frustration over such behavior on X .

"I'm technically an 'influencer' too," she wrote. "So maybe I'm allowed to say it: The US Open is not your personal content studio. Take the pictures. Make the TikToks. Have fun. But if your content is distracting the actual players, you've forgotten why you were invited in the first place."

The incident happened during Naomi Osaka 's opening-round game against world No. 101 Anastasia Zakharova at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Monday. While the game was going on, a group of people who appeared to be creators or influencers, sitting in a corporate hospitality suite directly behind the umpire's chair, began posing for photos. They even brought out and used bright, portable lights to properly capture whatever content they were creating, further creating a major visual distraction during active play.

And as a result, chair umpire Kader Nouni paused the match, turned toward the suite, and made an announcement over the microphone, asking them to stop and take their seats.

"Guys, please, in the suite behind me, thank you guys, please take your seat," he said.

The pause appeared to throw Osaka off her rhythm because when play resumed, her ball toss went awry, forcing her to apologize to Zakharova and reset. In fact, she ultimately lost that specific point, handing her opponent the advantage, although she eventually recovered to win the match in straight sets via two tiebreaks.

Reacting to the incident, head of US Open communications Brendan McIntyre defended the umpire's action while emphasizing that although fans and guests should be able to enjoy themselves at the tournament, their activities should not become a distraction to the players or interfere with the action on court.

"We want our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend the US Open, but we also need to ensure that it does not interfere with the action and competition on the court. These instances happen infrequently, and similar to when crowd noise reaches a certain level, our chair umpires have the ability to address the crowd when they occur," he said.

Some sections of fans are blaming the US Open's decision to invite accredited digital creators to the tournament, as the tournament reportedly approved passes for close to 100 digital creators for this year's event. This, they believe, has led to attendees who do not even care about the sport and therefore disregard strict tennis etiquette.

However, this tension with digital creators and influencers appears to be nothing new in the tennis world. In April 2025, Australian tennis player Daria Saville also expressed her frustration in a TikTok video, with her criticism focused on the corporate and marketing side of tennis, which she felt was increasingly giving more attention to major fashion and lifestyle brand deals involving influencers and tennis WAGs rather than the "actual, sweaty tennis players" who live the grind of the tour.

It is, however, quite understandable that the US Open extended invitations to digital creators in a bid to promote the tournament and make tennis more appealing, especially to a younger audience. Perhaps, in their focus on the benefits of bringing these creators closer to the action, they may not have fully considered that individuals who do not have an existing appreciation for tennis might end up struggling to understand or respect the etiquette expected during a live match.

articles.title: Group of influencers forces pause during US Open match with cringeworthy photoshoot in suite
articles.summary: A viral video shows credentialed influencers disrupting Naomi Osaka's U.S. Open match at Arthur Ashe Stadium, forcing the chair umpire to intervene.
articles.body: You could argue that the overwhelming number of influencers attending the U.S. Open are doing their job – having an influence on tennis' final Grand Slam of the year – but one could also say they're doing so in the worst, most negative way imaginable. Influencers and celebrities attending the U.S. Open simply to be seen is nothing new. After all, it's one of tennis' biggest events and is held in New York City. Posing for photos, hoping to be caught on a broadcast, or simply taking advantage of an invite for a luxury outing in a suite is one thing, but causing a pause in the action would be crossing a line. Well, in one of the most stereotypical 2026 moments imaginable, that's exactly what unfolded on Monday night at Arthur Ashe Stadium. AMERICAN TENNIS STAR AMANDA ANISIMOVA LEAVES FANS CONVINCED SHE DRANK BEER MID-MATCH WITH MYSTERY BEVERAGE As four-time Grand Slam winner Naomi Osaka was preparing to serve at deuce during the fourth game of the second set against Anastasia Zakharova, the chair umpire, Kader Nouni, took a moment to address a group that was causing a disturbance. "Guys, please, in the suite behind me, thank you guys, please take your seat," Nouni said to the audience. One video shared on TikTok that has gone viral across social media shows a woman using a large, very bright light to capture content during the middle of Osaka's match. Another video shows a large group of influencers in a suite collectively recording some sort of promotion, asking their audience, "Did you miss us?" Perhaps the most eye-opening aspect of the entire situation is that the United States Tennis Association (USTA) has brought this type of scenario upon itself at the U.S. Open. HATERS OF FASHION ATTACK ARYNA SABALENKA WITH 'STREETWALKER' INSULT SIMPLY BECAUSE SHE WORE FISHNET AT US OPEN Content creators, 54 to be exact, were credentialed as media for the first time at the 2025 U.S. Open. This year, that number of credentialed influencers is "close to 100," according to USTA director of media operations Jeanmarie Daly. "We realized we live in a world where traditional media and content creators reach different audiences in different ways," Daly told Front Office Sports ahead of this year's tournament. "Our goal for the program was to have the broadest possible spectrum of coverage for the tournament." articles.title: A Munar le falla el físico ante Rinderknech y se va del US Open
articles.standfirst: El balear pagó el cansancio del maratón del domingo con Terence Atmane
articles.summary: El balear pagó el cansancio del maratón del domingo con Terence Atmane
articles.body: La habitual chispa de Jaume Munar no estuvo presente este miércoles en la segunda ronda del US Open que le enfrentó a Arthur Rinderkench. El galo, vigésimo sexto cabeza de serie del cuadro, se mostró siempre más entero físicamente que su rival para cerrar un marcador de 7-6(4), 6-2 y 7-5. Las opciones de Munar para acceder a la tercera ronda se dilapidaron tras perder una renta de 5-2 en la manga inicial. Rinderknech, sin esperarlo, se encontró con una ventaja en el tanteo que no dejó escapar. Su víctima tuvo que llamar al fisioterapeuta de la organización para tratar su muslo derecho. Jaume venía de jugar casi cinco horas y con el tobillo vendado en el debut del domingo con Terence Atmane. Ese esfuerzo, sin duda, le pasó factura. El balear se centrará ahora en llegar en las mejores condiciones físicas a la serie de Copa Davis en Santiago de Chile contra el conjunto anfitrión los días 19 y 20 de septiembre. En juego, un billete para la Final a 8 de Bolonia. Munar disputará el punto del dobles al lado de Pedro Martínez.

articles.title: In 2010, two players walked onto Wimbledon’s Court 18 and played the longest match in tennis history. It didn’t end for three days, and the electronic scoreboard broke before they did
articles.summary: International Sports News: Explore the incredible journey of John Isner and Nicolas Mahut during their historic 2010 Wimbledon match, which lasted over 11 hours and broke multiple records, captivating fans worldwide.
articles.body: A tennis match that lasted 11 hours and five minutes, stretched across three days, produced 183 games, and eventually broke the electronic scoreboard sounds more like a story written for television than something that actually happened at Wimbledon. Yet that was precisely what unfolded when American John Isner and France's Nicolas Mahut met in the first round of the 2010 Championships. Their fifth set alone lasted eight hours and 11 minutes, longer than some entire professional matches, while both players repeatedly served to stay alive in a contest that seemed to have no natural ending. By the time Isner finally won 70-68, the match had become a record that remains untouched and a sporting absurdity that later inspired an HBO mockumentary.The match that refused to endIsner and Mahut began their first-round match on Court 18 at the All England Club on June 22, 2010, and neither could have known that they were about to spend three days playing one of the most extraordinary matches in tennis history.The opening four sets were already a serious contest, with Isner taking the first 6-4 before Mahut levelled with a 6-3 set. Mahut then edged the third 7-6, only for Isner to take the fourth by the same scoreline and force a deciding set.That was where the match became something entirely different.With the final set requiring a player to win by two clear games, neither man could create the decisive break. They held serve again and again as the score climbed through the 20s, 30s and 40s, with the match already far beyond anything Wimbledon had seen before.Play had originally been suspended because of fading natural light after the first four sets on June 22. The players returned the following day, but the fifth set still could not be completed, with darkness once again forcing the match to be stopped.They came back for a third day on June 24, still locked together.By then, even the electronic scoreboard had effectively conceded defeat. It stopped functioning at 47-47 in the fifth set because it had not been programmed to record a score that high.70-68: the fifth set that became its own matchThe numbers from the deciding set are difficult to comprehend even when written down.The fifth set lasted eight hours and 11 minutes and contained 138 games, with the players producing an astonishing 215 aces across the entire match: Isner hit 112 and Mahut 103.They also held serve for 168 consecutive games during the match, while Mahut had to serve to stay alive 63 times.There were only three service breaks in the entire contest.Eventually, after hours of holding serve, Isner finally won the 137th game of the fifth set to move ahead, before breaking Mahut in the following game to end the marathon at 70-68.The complete score read 6-4, 3-6, 6-7, 7-6, 70-68, with the match lasting 665 minutes, or 11 hours and five minutes.The final set alone was longer than the longest baseball game on record, which lasted eight hours and six minutes.The 183 games played overall were also 71 more than the previous highest total at Wimbledon, while the 138 games in the fifth set were 26 more than had been played in any other match.Isner and Mahut had also eclipsed the previous record for aces in a match, which had stood at 78, with their combined total of 215."I have never seen anything like it," Isner said afterwards, while the scale of what had happened was summed up by his prediction that "Nothing like this will ever happen again, ever."Neither player was quite the same afterwardsThe physical demands of the match became obvious immediately.Isner returned to the court for his second-round match against Dutchman Thiemo de Bakker, but lost in straight sets, with the effects of the three-day battle clearly still hanging over him.Mahut's defeat was equally extraordinary in its own way. Despite losing, he had produced one of the most remarkable individual performances in tennis history, with the two players setting records for points, games and aces that were unlikely to be approached again.The appeal of the match was not simply the final score, however, because as the fifth set moved beyond 50-50, both players were visibly exhausted while continuing to produce the physical effort required to keep the contest alive. Mahut repeatedly chased balls at full stretch, while Isner was visibly struggling between points, yet neither could find the small lapse that would finally end the contest.The fact that it was a first-round match on an outside court made the spectacle even stranger, with two players who were not among the sport's biggest global stars suddenly becoming the centre of attention as word spread about what was happening on Court 18.The match was so extraordinary that Wimbledon later commemorated it with a plaque outside Court 18.Isner and Mahut met again in the first round at Wimbledon in 2011, but there was no repeat marathon, with Isner winning in straight sets.The record changed tennisThe Isner-Mahut marathon was possible because of the Grand Slam rules in place at the time, which required the final set to continue until one player established a two-game advantage.That system has since changed at the major tournaments, making another 70-68 deciding set increasingly difficult to imagine.Wimbledon now uses a tie-break when the final set reaches 12-12, while the Australian Open uses a first-to-10-point super tie-break at 6-6. The French Open has also retained the advantage-set principle in its deciding sets.Isner himself would later find himself at the centre of another Wimbledon marathon. In the 2018 semi-finals, he lost to South Africa's Kevin Anderson 7-6, 6-7, 7-6, 4-6, 24-26 after six hours and 36 minutes.That match became the fourth-longest in tennis history and the second-longest at a Grand Slam, but the repeated marathon matches contributed to Wimbledon eventually introducing its fifth-set tie-break.Other records remain well behind Isner and Mahut's mark. The longest Grand Slam final in the Open Era was the 2012 Australian Open final, where Novak Djokovic defeated Rafael Nadal 5-7, 6-4, 6-2, 6-7, 7-5 after five hours and 53 minutes.The longest women's singles match lasted six hours and 31 minutes, with Vicki Nelson beating Jean Hepner 6-4, 7-6 at the 1984 Central Fidelity Banks International tournament.The longest doubles match came at the 2013 Davis Cup, when Tomas Berdych and Lukas Rosol defeated Switzerland's Stanislas Wawrinka and Marco Chiudinelli 6-4, 5-7, 6-4, 6-7, 24-22 after seven hours and two minutes.None came close to the 11-hour, three-day ordeal in south-west London.From Wimbledon absurdity to HBOThe story eventually travelled well beyond tennis.The 2010 marathon helped inspire HBO's "7 Days in Hell", a mockumentary starring Andy Samberg and Kit Harington about two fictional tennis players locked in an impossibly long Grand Slam match.Samberg later recalled watching the real-life Isner-Mahut match with writer Murray Miller and joking that somebody should make a film about a tennis match that simply never ends.That joke became the 2015 HBO film, which exaggerated the premise to comic extremes, but its starting point was very real: two players, three days, 11 hours and five minutes, 183 games and a fifth set that reached 70-68 before anyone could finally walk off Court 18.More than 16 years later, the Isner-Mahut match remains the Guinness World Record holder for the longest professional tennis match ever played.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jódar frena ante Bu y se despide en su estreno neoyorquino
articles.standfirst: El madrileño, siempre por detrás, cede en tres rápidos sets y se aleja del 'top10' y las ATP Finals de Turín
articles.summary: El madrileño, siempre por detrás, cede en tres rápidos sets y se aleja del 'top10' y las ATP Finals de Turín
articles.body: Rafa Jódar llegaba con toda la ilusión del mundo a su primer US Open entre los profesionales. Había ganado dos años antes entre los júniors. Es casi todo nuevo para él en sus primeros ocho meses en el circuito, pero su regularidad le permitía soñar con las ATP Finals de Turín y optar ya a ingresar en el 'top10' mundial. Nadie ha sumado más triunfos que él esta campaña, con un total de 49. Jódar tuvo ese mal día en la oficina en el peor momento, el que debutaba en el grande neoyorquino. Su verdugo fue Yunchaokete Bu, por 6-2, 6-1 y 6-1. La organización programó el partido en la pista 17, más conocida por estar pegada al Corona Park y atraer el humo de la marihuana que tanto molesta a los tenistas. La más de hora de parón por la lluvia, con 4-1 en el tercer set para Bu, tampoco ayudó a la reacción del decimosegundo cabeza de serie del cuadro. Con un 52 por ciento de primeros saques y 37 errores no forzados se hacía difícil pensar en darle la vuelta ante un Yunchaokete iluminado. Hasta siete veces le robó el saque a su oponente. Jódar pareció cansado desde el primer punto, empapado y afectado por el 70 por ciento de humedad de la ciudad de Nueva York. Su lenguaje corporal no era el mejor (se agachaba) y el 'lucky loser' chino se dio cuenta de ello muy rápido. Afincado en España y tutelado por Ricardo Ojeda, sabía lo que tenía que hacer en cada momento. Rafa mandaba a encordar una raqueta tras otra buscando una solución. Bu, que ni se inmuta, se mostraba intocable al servicio contra un adversario que es el cuarto mejor restador del circuito. El madrileño no se despedía en la primera ronda de un torneo desde el Masters 1000 de Indian Wells, a principios de marzo, cuando cedió con el chileno Alejandro Tabilo. Volverán a verse las caras el 19 y 20 de septiembre en la serie de Copa Davis en Santiago de Chile, con un billete en juego para la Final a 8 de Bolonia. Un aprendizaje más para Rafa, que volverá más fuerte y más hecho.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Daniil Medvedev progresses to third round despite bird interruption
articles.summary: An interruption from a pair of birds ruffles Daniil Medvedev's feathers but fails to disrupt the seventh seed as he eases into the US Open third round with a dominant victory over Sebastian Gorzny.
articles.body:
An interruption from a pair of birds ruffled Daniil Medvedev's feathers but could not disrupt the seventh seed as he eased into the US Open third round with a dominant victory over Sebastian Gorzny.

The two birds settled down on the net for a closer look at the action midway through a second-set rally, with play continuing around them for several strokes before the chair umpire called for the point to be replayed.

Medvedev, who placed the incident in his "top five" most unusual experiences at the New York major, was visibly stunned by the decision which came just after he thought he had won the point with a cross-court forehand.

"This is very bad," the 2021 champion said as he remonstrated at the umpire on court.

Russia's Medvedev is no stranger to losing his composure on court, notably receiving a fine of almost £31,500 at last year's US Open for an extraordinary meltdown during his first-round defeat to Benjamin Bonzi.

As recently as last month's Winston-Salem Open, where he again lost in the opening round, he spent a disconsolate change of ends questioning his future in the sport, musing "maybe I should start a career in pickleball".

However, the 30-year-old, who had already flown through the first set in just 21 minutes, quickly brushed aside the avian interruption to complete a straightforward 6-1 6-3 7-5 win over American wildcard Gorzny, the world number 731.

"I saw [the birds] straight away," Medvedev - who will play Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech in the third round - said in his on-court interview.

"I thought the point would stop straight away but it didn't.

"Then we play for 45 seconds and the moment I hit the winner we say stop. I'm like, 'Why? We played for 45 seconds!'.

"But it's okay. I was not happy with the decision but it is was it is. You can't do anything with it.

"The situation was pretty crazy but I love this court, I'm happy to win, to stay in the US Open, to stay in New York for longer."

Gorzny was making his Grand Slam debut at the US Open, seven years after being given a 5% chance to live after being taken ill at the USTA Boys' 16s National Championships in Michigan.

Then aged 15, Gorzny suffered a seizure in the night and was placed in an induced coma for four days.

"The doctors aren't really sure what it was actually, but they're guessing a mosquito bite that led to some type of brain infection: meningitis, encephalitis," Gorzny told the ATP before the US Open.

A former Wimbledon boys' doubles champion, Gorzny, the world number 731, earned his place in the main draw at Flushing Meadows by winning the USTA American Collegiate Player Wildcard Playoff in June.

articles.title: Ben Shelton avoids U.S. Open upset scare from unseeded Hubert Hurkacz in close four-set victory
articles.summary: Shelton moves on to the third round at the U.S. Open for the fourth time in his career.
articles.body:
Wednesday's slate of men's singles matches was highlighted by the top-seeded American Ben Shelton taking on the unseeded Hubert Hurkacz from Poland.

Shelton - seeded 8th overall in the men's draw - has now had back-to-back four-set matchups in the 2026 U.S. Open.

The American bested Hurkacz on Wednesday, 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (7-3), and 7-5. Shelton was overcome with emotion after the close match and had quite the celebration after clinching the final point.

The 2026 U.S. Open hasn't been the smoothest sailing to the start of a major for the American star. Shelton dropped the first set of his first-round matchup against Tallon Griekspoor, but was able to bounce back with three straight sets to take the match.

After Wednesday's victory, Shelton is through to the third round and will face the winner of Denis Shavlov and Luca Van Assche, both unseeded, who play later on Wednesday.

This is the sixth U.S. Open of the 23-year-old's career. His best finish so far came in 2023, when he made it all the way to the semifinals. Shelton faced No. 2 Novak Djokovic, but lost in straight sets, 3-6, 2-6, 6-7 (4-7).

The third round has been a tough one for Shelton at this Grand Slam. He has reached the round three times before this year, and has lost in two of those appearances, including each of the last two years.

Shelton is one of six Americans who were seeded in the 2026 U.S. Open draw, joining Learner Tien (No. 14), Taylor Fritz (No. 9), Frances Tiafoe (No. 11), Brandon Nakashima (No. 16), Tommy Paul (No. 20).

For Hurkacz, it is another early exit from the final tennis major of the year. He has competed in eight U.S. Opens now, but is still looking for his first trip to the third round.

In his career, his best major finish came at Wimbledon in 2021, when he reached the semifinals before losing to Matteo Berrettini in four sets.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Katie Boulter blown away by Karolina Muchova
articles.summary: British No 1 broken in every service game and bageled in second set as US Open campaign unravels at hands of Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova in under an hour; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The British No 1 was broken in all seven of her service games in a chastening 6-1 6-0 defeat inside 58 minutes on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

Boulter traded breaks with Muchova at the start of the first set only for the 2026 Wimbledon finalist to pull clear and put on a clinic for her beleaguered opponent.

Boulter double faulted eight times and produced 22 unforced errors in a nightmare, error-strewn performance that left her hopes of progressing in tatters.

"It was a tough day at the office for Boulter, and that is where Muchova deserves so much credit. She is such an all-round player. The focus was definitely on Muchova rather than what Boulter didn't do.

"The highlight reel from the match was outstanding. There were so many incredible shots and great rallies. She's got the variation, using the little short chip cross-court, following the ball in and knocking off volleys at the net. She can do anything.

"She has reached the French Open and Wimbledon finals and is great on hard courts. If she can stay healthy, she has the experience, mentality, confidence and belief to win one of these tournaments one day."

"You've got to focus on the positives, and that was how well Muchova played.

"She showed us every trick in the book. She has so much in her repertoire. She's playing with a lot of confidence for something who hasn't played a lot since Wimbledon.

"Not a good day at the office for Boulter."

"Karolina Muchova has yet to win a Grand Slam in her career but played some exceptional tennis. On that evidence, she has brilliant potential in this tournament.

"A day to forget for Katie Boulter. She just wasn't there and lost her serve seven times out of seven. That does not give you a chance."

Choinski four-day first-round run brought to end

Britain's Jan Choinski made it to day four at the US Open, but was still a first-round casualty.

The towering German-born 30-year-old was beaten in straight sets by fellow beanpole, Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp.

Getting to the first Wednesday at Flushing Meadows is usually a notable achievement for a British player.

But Choinski's stay at the tournament was only extended after his first-round match was pushed back by the rain in New York.

A handful of players were already through to round three by the time Choinski took to the court, but he was soundly beaten in the big-serving battle 6-3 6-1 7-6 (5) in just under two hours.

Choinski is coached by his girlfriend Sophia, who was shouting encouragement from his players' box.

He said: "She always tries to help me, tries to keep me positive, for sure.

"In the first set it was quite good, I had some chances but from that point it got tough.

"The guy was playing aggressively and she just keeps me fighting and motivated. But in a match like that it's quite tough."

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Katie Boulter wins just one game in 58-minute US Open defeat by Karolina Muchova
articles.summary: British number one Katie Boulter is dumped out in the second round of the US Open as she wins just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova.
articles.body:
British number one Katie Boulter endured a "bad day at the office" as she won just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova in the US Open second round.

The match, originally scheduled to be played on one of the outer courts, was moved to the 14,000-capacity Louis Armstrong Stadium after heavy rain in New York.

But fans who had counted themselves lucky to have gained a third match on their day session ticket may have been left feeling short-changed, as Boulter fell to a swift 6-1 6-0 defeat by the Czech seventh seed.

"Ultimately, it was a bad day at the office – times two," said Boulter.

"I struggled with the conditions. I struggled with the roof, the noise, I let things distract me.

"I let it get to me. I'm not usually aware of everything going on. It made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. I have to deal with it better."

Fellow Briton Jacob Fearnley also failed to reach the third round as he suffered a 6-3 6-3 3-6 6-3 loss to Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry.

But Francesca Jones had better fortune as she returned to win her first-round match against Poland's Magda Linette after it was interrupted by rain on Tuesday.

Boulter's serve let her down as she hit eight double faults and no aces, while she won just 33% of points behind her first serve.

Unable to fend off any of the seven break points she faced, the 30-year-old was not helped by an unforced error count of 22 compared to just four winners.

In comparison, Wimbledon runner-up Muchova landed 14 winners and just nine unforced errors as she impressed with smart drop shots and piercing groundstrokes.

"I would be really humbled [if I was Boulter], I would sit down with my team and say 'OK, we need to change something big time'," former world number five Daniela Hantuchova told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"First of all, it was very obvious today that it was the serve. I feel like it needs to be cleared up because she was losing the rhythm and not using her legs. That's the number one thing.

"If I am Boulter, I would be on the practice court tomorrow. If she still wants to invest everything into her tennis then she needs to be on the court."

Boulter has had plenty to celebrate in her personal life this summer after marrying Australia's Alex de Minaur, the world number seven, in July.

However, it has been a disappointing tennis season for the world number 62, with just two wins across the four Grand Slam tournaments.

Since suffering a first-round exit at Wimbledon, Boulter has won just two of the six matches she has played.

Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round

Jones had won the first set 6-4 against Linette, ranked 82nd, when the rain put a halt to proceedings on Tuesday night.

When the pair returned on Wednesday, it was Linette who appeared fresher as she raced to a 5-0 lead and wrapped up the second set in 28 minutes.

"I've never been quite in this position so I was nervous with how I'd quite feel about coming back out," Jones told Sky Sports afterwards.

"I thought I'd maybe handle it better than the score reflects."

Jones rallied back in the decider, claiming the decisive break at 2-1 before completing the victory - just her second at Grand Slam level.

She will play either American 14th seed Iva Jovic or Poland's Magdalena Frech in the second round on Thursday.

"[I'm] really grateful that I just managed to pull through," said Jones.

"She came out all guns blazing - it was incredible how she was playing until about 4-0 and then it started to equal out. But in that situation, hats off if they can sustain that, I just tried to show my northern grit, stick in there and do what I can."

Fearnley had produced a remarkable five-set comeback against Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round, but the British lucky loser's fortune ran out against Etcheverry.

The world number 32 recovered from losing the third set and falling a break behind in the fourth, while Fearnley's 57 unforced errors and 11 double faults ultimately proved costly.

Fellow Briton Jan Choinski, meanwhile, failed to reach round two as he fell to a 6-3 6-1 7-6 (7-5) defeat by Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in a first-round match that had also been pushed back to Wednesday because of the rain at Flushing Meadows.

articles.title: US Open under the influence: content creators spark debate
articles.summary: Jessica Pegula is all in favor of bringing more fans into tennis, but the world number three said Wednesday it's important to keep the focus on the game.The...
articles.body:
Jessica Pegula is all in favor of bringing more fans into tennis, but the world number three said Wednesday it's important to keep the focus on the game.

The US Tennis Association doubled down this year on credentials awarded to content creators -- reportedly handing out almost 100 after making 54 available in 2025 to amplify the tournament's presence on social media.

The influencers focus not just on tennis, but on fashion, food and lifestyle topics that are now an inextricable part of the game.

But the embrace of content creators sparked some backlash when the chair umpire of Naomi Osaka's first round match against Anastasia Zakharova had to shush a group in a courtside suite who appeared to be conducting a noisy photo shoot during a point.

"I think I can appreciate, you know, the influencers coming and kind of showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.

"I think that's something that the US Open has utilized a lot as far as food and drinks and things to do and the shops. That part is part of a fan experience and something that people might not know and make them want to go.

"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos like that, when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.

"People are down there trying to perform, and it's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful," Pegula concluded.

Russian Daniil Medvedev, a former world number one and the 2021 US Open champion, said the more focus on the sport the better, and any problems can be ironed out.

"In general, the more the sport grows, the better it is," Medvedev said.

"For sure, if it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee.

"(It) can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens. But I'm pretty sure as well, even them, you know, maybe one time they do it, and then someone tells them not to do it.

"I think (there is) a lot of more upside than downside, so go for it."

articles.title: US Open: Aryna Sabalenka flies past Polina Iatcenko in 54 minutes to reach third round as dominant start continues
articles.summary: Aryna Sabalenka wasn't messing around on Wednesday night at Arthur Ashe Stadium.
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka isn't having any issues whatsoever in New York.

Sabalenka, after significant issues at earlier Grand Slams this year, rolled into the third round of the US Open with ease on Wednesday night. She cruised to a dominant 6-1, 6-1 win over Polina Iatcenko at Arthur Ashe Stadium. And she only needed 54 minutes to do so.

It marked her second straight sets victory so far at the US Open, following a slightly less dominant win over Camila Osorio in the opening round. Sabalenka will now take on Kamilla Rakhimova in the third round. Rakhimova beat Oksana Selekhmeteva in straight sets in her second-round match.

Sabalenka looked unstoppable in the first set, and rolled to a dominant 5-0 lead before Iatcenko managed to find a little bit of stability in the match. Up until that point. Sabalenka had only dropped seven total points. There was nothing Iatcenko could do.

Iatcenko got on the board finally with a narrow win in the sixth game, but that was all she could manage. Sabalenka won the next four points, and wasted no time doing it, to close out the first set in less than 25 minutes.

The second set didn't get any petter for Iatcenko. Sabalenka broke her serve to get things started, and then rolled through the second game without giving up a point to take a 2-0 lead instantly.

Sabalenka gave up a single game again in the second set, but that was it. She responded by winning seven straight points to take control out the match back almost instantly after that.

Sabalenka has won three singles titles already in 2026, and she made it all the way to the Australian Open final back in January. But the other two Grand Slam outings weren't great. She was knocked out of the French Open in the quarterfinals, and Naomi Osaka got her in straight sets at Wimbledon. After her French Open loss, Sabalenka was so frustrated that she said she just wanted "to quit tennis right now" altogether .

Clearly, her issues in Europe didn't carry over into the US Open. Sabalenka maintained her No. 1 WTA ranking and was the favorite entering the final Grand Slam of the season. Wednesday's match was just further proof of how much of a dominant force she is in the sport, and how hard its going to be to slow her down if this continues.

Sabalenka is off to the perfect start in New York.

articles.body:
Jodar was tripped up at the first hurdle of his maiden ‌campaign in New York, as the Spanish 12th seed failed to find his rhythm and fell 6-2 6-1 ‌6-1 to Bu.

Back at the site of his junior triumph two ​years ago, 19-year-old Jodar looked unusually out of sorts after his first-round clash was delayed by a day due to ​rain, with a flurry of unforced errors in defeat.

Jodar, one of the fastest-rising talents in the ‌men's game after going from 362nd in the world to 13th over the past year, continued to struggle for answers and even sent several of his rackets to be re-strung in a bid to change his fortunes.

But it proved futile, with ⁠the 24-year-old Bu refusing to loosen his grip on the contest ​as he took the first set before sealing the second set after another unforced ​error from Jodar to silence a vocal contingent of Spanish supporters ​on Court 17.

World No 124 Bu completed the upset after an hour-long rain ⁠delay, securing his maiden Grand Slam main-draw victory on his seventh attempt.

"After I lost in qualifying, ⁠I took a day off but I ⁠saw a few guys pull out, so I took the decision to come back and tried to do some ‌work in case I could play. Yesterday, they told me I could... when I heard that, I was super excited."

Jodar responds to question about his shoelaces

Jodar was asked about people discussing his shoelaces breaking during matches on social media and if he's more aware now of how he might be perceived online.

Journalist: "Tough one. I'm sure you've probably seen online throughout the year some people talking about how your shoelaces break and things like that. I'm just wondering, are you more aware now of how you'll just be perceived online depending on what you said?"

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka continues title defence with one of the quickest Grand Slam wins of her career
articles.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka cruises into the US Open third round before a spiky exchange with a journalist.
articles.body:
Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka earned one of the quickest Grand Slam wins of her career with a 53-minute pummelling of US Open debutant Polina Iatcenko in the second round.

However, the world number one did not look entirely happy even as she swept aside Iatcenko - then had a spiky exchange with a reporter in her post-match news conference.

Sabalenka, 28, is aiming to win her first major title of a strange season where she has enjoyed spectacular success but is now looking to recover from a recent dip.

Coasting to a 6-1 6-1 victory over 22-year-old qualifier Iatcenko did not offer a true test of where Sabalenka's level is.

But the ruthless manner in which she secured victory will certainly boost confidence as she looks to complete a rare 'three-peat' of US Open titles.

"I'm happy with the level I played, happy with the focus and happy to be through this match," said Sabalenka, who will play Uzbekistan's Kamilla Rakhimova in the third round.

Boulter wins one game in 58-minute US Open defeat

Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round

Sabalenka knows she must the lift the trophy in New York again to stand any chance of preventing Elena Rybakina taking her position at the top of the rankings.

Even if Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still rise to the summit by reaching the semi-finals.

Sabalenka losing the top spot seemed unthinkable after a storming start to the season, reaching the Australian Open final and winning the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back.

Losing to Rybakina in Melbourne was Sabalenka's only defeat in her first 27 matches of 2026. After completing the Sunshine Double, her win-loss record leading into the US Open dropped to 17-7 and she has only reached one WTA semi-final in the past five months.

Before the final Grand Slam of the season, Sabalenka admitted she had been "dealing with several things" in a period which she knows was far below her best.

And, after beating Iatcenko, Sabalenka took umbrage with what she perceived to be a suggestion from a reporter that she had been attending "lots of parties" in the build-up to the US Open.

"What kind of question is that? Just because I posted some activities with brands, you think that I've been partying [and] not training?" countered Sabalenka.

Asked if she was "getting serious" now the tournament was under way, she said: "Oh yeah, I wasn't serious before that. Next question."

Sabalenka's pace and power was too much for world number 160 Iatcenko, who managed just three winners compared to the 24 put away by the top seed.

Iatcenko looked a bundle of nerves in the biggest match of her career, but composed herself to get on the scoreboard for 5-1 and immediately broke out into a relieved smile.

It was merely respite as Sabalenka held to love in fewer than 90 seconds to clinch the opening set.

Despite only being on court for 24 minutes, Iatchenko decided she wanted a bathroom break to change her kit - but more likely for a mental reset than anything else.

Sabalenka kept loose while she waited by practising her serves and maintained her rhythm as she surged a double break ahead for 3-0 in the second set.

It was not all plain-sailing for Sabalenka as she lost serve in a sloppy fourth game, but reasserted her authority with two more breaks as Iatchenko was taught a harsh lesson.

The Russian can console herself with the knowledge she has gained valuable experience against the world number one on the biggest court on the planet - and a bumper paycheck.

Coming into the US Open, she had earned $300,000 (£220,000) in her career but takes another $190,000 home from New York to reinvest into her future.

Earlier on Wednesday, third seed Pegula continued her quest for a maiden Grand Slam singles title with a comfortable victory over fellow American Sofia Kenin.

Pegula also has a shot of replacing Sabalenka as world number one if she wins the title, as does fourth seed Coco Gauff, and kept her dream alive with a 6-3 6-1 win.

There were also straight-set wins for Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova, two-time major semi-finalist Marta Kostyuk and teenage American sensation Iva Jovic as the pattern of few shocks in the women's draw over the opening two rounds continued.

articles.summary: Tennis News: Peruvian tennis player Ignacio Buse earned his first US Open match win on Wednesday, adding another chapter to his family's history at the tournament .
articles.body: Peruvian tennis player Ignacio Buse earned his first US Open match win on Wednesday, adding another chapter to his family's history at the tournament nearly seven decades after his grandfather last won a match there.The 22-year-old, seeded 32nd, defeated American Marcos Giron 3-6, 6-3, 6-3, 6-7(6), 6-1 in a match that lasted three hours and 48 minutes on Court Six.Buse sealed the win with a backhand volley, which was followed by celebrations from his team and fans in the stands.“It's difficult to find the calm in those situations, but in the fifth set, I just tried to recover mentally,” Ignacio said, as quoted by news agency Reuters.“It's a mental battle out there. I just stayed calm. It's a very special moment.”The victory also brought back memories of his grandfather, Eduardo Buse, who last won a match at the tournament in 1958.Although Ignacio never met his grandfather, he has now matched a family achievement that dates back 68 years.Eduardo Buse, along with his twin brother Enrique, is remembered in Peruvian tennis history through Lima's Estadio Hermanos Buse. He first played at the tournament in 1942.His last US Open win came in 1958, when he defeated American Edward Atkinson in five sets in the opening round.At that time, the tournament was known as the US Championships and was played on the outdoor grass courts of the West Side Tennis Club in Forest Hills, New York. articles.summary: El murciano levanta un set en contra y avisa que su físico está de vuelta para ganar el título en Nueva York
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz reconocía tras ganar en la primera ronda a Roman Safiullin que había pensado cómo iba a responder su cuerpo si el partido se hubiera alargado a cuatro o cinco sets. Esa prueba le esperaba en la sesión nocturna del miércoles en el US Open ante el combativo Jaime Faria, que se rindió finalmente con un tanteo de 4-6, 6-0, 6-3 y 6-2. Después de perder la manga inicial, el campeón de siete 'grandes', dos de ellos en la Arthur Ashe neoyorquina, reaccionó cómo sólo lo hacen unos pocos elegidos. Perdió cinco juegos más. Su cuerpo está como siempre, como cuando decía sentirse "como un toro". Usa, por precaución, la malla en el brazo derecho, pero le pega y mucho a la bola. La estadística no suele mentir y menos en el tenis: 43 golpes ganadores. Hasta ocho juegos seguidos se anotó el murciano en la continuación ante el fervor de una grada entregada a su causa. En el segundo set, anotó el rosco 22º de su carrera profesional. El tenis ha echado mucho de menos a Alcaraz. Pero él también ha echado en falta el deporte de la raqueta, la alta competición y los estadios llenos. El Abierto de los Estados Unidos reúne todo eso. A Carlitos le gusta ganar siempre, pero, sobre todo, en los Grand Slam, los que marcan la trayectoria y el recuerdo de las leyendas. No es casualidad que encadene 16 triunfos en los 'majors' desde la consecución de su segunda corona en la ciudad de los rascacielos hace un año. Por el camino han pasado muchas cosas, la lesión en la muñeca derecha por encima de todas ellas porque le ha dejado más de cuatro meses sin competir. Si algo caracteriza a Faria es que no se rinde. Por eso es el segundo jugador con más victorias en el presente curso, las mismas de Alexander Zverev, y sólo superado por las 49 de Rafa Jódar. "Tenis de alto nivel", le decía Samuel López a su pupilo tras lograr el segundo 'break' del tercer set y situar un marcador de 3-1 a su favor. Estaba en modo remontada y lo estaba consiguiendo sin dejarse excesivo tiempo. A pesar de la remontada, Alcaraz, un perfeccionista, no estaba del todo contento con su tenis y así se lo hacía saber a los suyos. La amenaza de lluvia provocó que se cerrara la Arthur Ashe para poder terminar sin sobresaltos de última hora. Yibing Wu, el 113 del ranking a sus 26 años, será el adversario del número tres mundial este viernes por un puesto en los octavos. Wu pasó a la historia de su país en febrero de 2023 al convertirse en el primer chimo en ganar un titulo ATP. Fue en el torneo de Dallas. En el horizonte, unos octavos con Alexander Bublik (15) o Tommy Paul (20).. Pero eso será para otro día.

articles.title: Wu, el tenista que dejó el bádminton porque la red estaba muy alta, foto con Yao Ming, campeón júnior...
articles.standfirst: El tenista de Hangzhou se convirtió en 2023 en el primer chino en ganar un título ATP en Dallas
articles.summary: El tenista de Hangzhou se convirtió en 2023 en el primer chino en ganar un título ATP en Dallas
articles.body: El nombre de Yibing Wu vuelve a sonar fuerte en los vestuarios del tenis porque él será el rival de Carlos Alcaraz este viernes en la tercera ronda del US Open. El chino se ganó ese derecho tras derrotar al húngaro Fabian Marozsan. La carrera de Wu tiene un antes y un después de febrero de 2023. Fue entonces cuando se convirtió en el primer chino en ganar un titulo ATP tras imponerse a John Isner en la final del Open 250 de Dallas. Wu, de 26 años y en el puesto 113 del ranking, empezó con otra raqueta, la de bádminton. Pero dejó ese deporte por lo alta que estaba la red. "Siempre he confiado en mis posibilidades y creo que hubiera sido un buen jugador de bádminton o un buen estudiante", dice. Pronto destacó en categorías inferiores, como número uno júnior y campeón del US Open de la categoría en 2017. Allí ya le echó sus redes la multinacional IMG, que también lleva las riendas de la carrera de Alcaraz y antes de otros como Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer o Maria Sharapova. Yibing, natural de Hangzhou, estuvo más de un año sin poder ver a su familia por culpa de la mala situación con el coronavirus en China. No podía volver a casa. Uno de los momentos imborrables en la vida de Wu fue cuando conoció a uno de sus referentes de la infancia, el gigante Yao Ming. "Coincidimos en un acto con patrocinadores y nos hicimos una foto. Él es la gran estrella del deporte en China, es una leyenda. Creo que es más alto incluso que Isner", explica. Su ídolo de infancia fue Kevin Durant y Wu cuenta las razones: "Mi primer recuerdo de un partido de baloncesto fueron las finales de la NBA de 2012 entre Oklahoma y Miami. Allí descubrí a Durant. Me encanta su puesta en escena, que nunca sepas lo que siente. Yo me identifico un poco con él en la pista, es elegante y no hace tonterías". Poco amante de la fiesta es un amante de la música asiática y la cocina: "Me divierte ver programas de cocina e intentar repetir lo que enseñan. Aunque me salga fatal, disfruto del proceso. Es una manera de distraerme después de los entrenamientos".

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz fights back to beat Jaime Faria as injury comeback in New York continues
articles.summary: Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz fights back from a set down to reach the US Open third round on his injury comeback.
articles.body:
Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz avoided the prospect of an early US Open exit by fighting back from a set down against Portugal's Jaime Faria.

Alcaraz, 23, needed time to find his rhythm in the second-round contest as he continues to make his comeback from a long-term wrist injury.

But the Spanish second seed asserted his authority to win 4-6 6-0 6-3 6-2 against world number 72 Faria in the New York night session.

Alcaraz fighting off two break points in the first game of the second set proved to be pivotal.

"It was a tough match for me. I felt great in the first set, but I didn't take time and that cost me," said the seven-time Grand Slam champion.

"After that I tried to be focused, stay calm and think the good things will happen."

Going into the final major of the season, everyone wondered how Alcaraz would fare in his first tournament since mid-April following an injury to his playing right wrist.

The latest evidence showed the two-time US Open winner is beginning to gather momentum.

Alcaraz said he was playing "normal" in a straight-set win over Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first round and reiterated after beating Faria that he is not holding back on his forehand.

"I know once I step on the court, I've just got to go for it every time. I've got to feel normal," said Alcaraz.

"I have to hit like I was hitting before the injury. I'm feeling great. There is no reason to be afraid and not hitting normal."

Sabalenka earns 53-minute US Open win - but tension still shows

Boulter wins one game in 58-minute US Open defeat

Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round

After coming through his opening match with little fuss, the questions then turned to how Alcaraz would pull up physically two days later.

Sweeping aside 23-year-old Faria answered those emphatically, although Alcaraz knows the tests will get tougher if he is able to move further through the draw.

As well as the likelihood of facing opponents ranked much higher than Safiullin and Faria, it will be interesting to see how his body continues to react to playing more five-set matches in quick succession after such a long absence.

On whether he wished he had been quicker against Faria, Alcaraz said: "At the end, I realised that playing four sets was really good for me to test everything physically, to test my body, how I feel, and how I'm going to feel tomorrow after this match."

With his fierce rival Jannik Sinner missing from New York through injury, and 24-time major champion Novak Djokovic already out, Alcaraz might increasingly fancy his chances of going all the way in a draw which looks to be wide open.

Alcaraz's next challenge will be overcoming China's Wu Yibing, who is ranked 113th in the world, in the last 32.

Meanwhile, American 20th seed Tommy Paul - a potential opponent for Alcaraz in the fourth round - continued his progress with a 6-2 6-3 5-7 6-4 victory over Croatia's Dino Prizmic.

Paul goes on to face Kazakh 15th seed Alexander Bublik, who cruised past French veteran Adrian Mannarino in a 6-3 6-1 6-1 win.

Eighth seed Ben Shelton continued his own quest to become the first American men's champion since Andy Roddick in 2003 with a 6-3 5-7 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 victory over Poland's Hubert Hurkacz.

Two-time semi-finalist Frances Tiafoe, another home favourite, demonstrated his great form with a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 7-5 win against Japan's Rei Sakamoto, but Spanish 12th seed Rafael Jodar was the biggest casualty in the men's draw on day four as he was beaten 6-2 6-1 6-1 by Chinese world number 124 Bu Yunchaokete.

articles.body:
The two-time defending champion thrashed Russian qualifier Polina Iatcenko 6-1 6-1 in 53 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The Belarusian, who had faced a similar line of questioning ​after her first-round win , fired back that her off-court appearances had not come at the expense of her preparations ​for the Grand Slam.

Sabalenka - a regular poster on social media at the various events she attends and with the brands she works with - replied: "You guys are, like, a joke.

When the reporter responded: "I'm saying that there are a lot of events and things like that. I'm not saying you go to the parties," Sabalenka interrupted: "You literally said that. Next question."

The reporter replied: "For everyone who is unclear, I'm not suggesting that Aryna is having fun at these parties."

"I'm saying that she makes a lot of appearances and there's a lot to do and lots of events, OK?" said the reporter.

She was then asked: "So, now that the tournament has started, do you find you're getting quite serious and combative?"

Sabalanka replied: "Oh, yeah, I wasn't serious before that. Next question. Think before you say stuff."

The world No 1, seeking a third straight ​title in New York to ‌emulate Serena Williams and Chris Evert, faces Uzbekistan's Kamilla Rakhimova on Friday looking for a 17th consecutive win at Flushing Meadows.

Carlos Alcaraz's comeback ‌from a long wrist injury layoff gathered momentum as ‌he came from behind to outclass Portugal's Jaime Faria ​4-6 6-0 6-3 6-2 and reach the third round.

The defending champion rebounded from an early deficit by winning eight straight games and beat Faria.

"After that I just tried to be focused, tried to stay calm and I'm thinking that good things are going to happen again," said Alcaraz, who is on a 16-match winning streak in Grand Slam tournaments.

Peruvian Ignacio Buse added a new chapter to ‌his family's US Open story as he came through a five-setter to ‌earn a maiden victory and follow in the footsteps of his grandfather Eduardo, ​who last won a match at the tournament in 1958.

The 32nd seed beat American Marcos Giron ​3-6 6-3 6-3 6-7(6) 6-1 after three hours ‌and 48 minutes on Court Six, finishing off the match with a backhand ​volley to spark loud cheers from his team and fans in the stands.

"It's difficult to find the calm in those ​situations, but in the fifth set, I just ⁠tried to recover mentally," Ignacio ⁠said.

"It's a mental battle out there. I just stayed calm. It's a very special moment."

Stefanos Tsitsipas survived a battle ​against South Africa's Lloyd Harris, recovering from a set down to clinch a 6-7 (1-7) 6-3 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 victory. The Greek player, who stunned 10th seed Arthur Fils in the first round, next faces Czech 18th seed Jiri Lehecka .

American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe beat Japanese qualifier Rei Sakamoto ‌6-3 7-6 (7-2) 7-5, keeping alive the country's hopes of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion in New York.

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz, el Odiseo del tenis: lo que hay detrás de su nueva celebración como un arquero

articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz celebró como un arquero su triunfo ante Jaime Faria en el US Open
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz celebró su triunfo en cuatro sets ante el portugués Jaime Faria lanzando una flecha como un arquero, al más puro estilo de Odiseo (Matt Damon) en la película 'La Odisea' de Christopher Nolan. El tenista español lanzó una flecha a la grada a sus hermanos Sergio y Jaime. Alcaraz explicó el origen de su nueva celebración del arquero: "Mis dos hermanos pequeños están aquí y me pidieron que lanzara una flecha. Así que ha sido un momento para ellos". Tras el partido Carlos Alcaraz reconoció que haber disputado un partido a cuatro sets contra Jaime Faria ha sido "algo muy bueno". "No voy a mentir, quería que terminase rápido, pero luego me he dado cuenta de que jugar cuatro sets era algo muy bueno para mí, porque me iba a permitir ponerlo todo a prueba físicamente: comprobar cómo respondía mi cuerpo, cómo me sentía y cómo me encontraré mañana después de un partido de cuatro sets", explicó. Alcaraz, que acabó ganando 4-6, 6-0, 6-3 y 6-2 en 2 horas y 40 minutos, reconoció que "estoy contento de haber podido jugar un buen tenis durante los cuatro sets". Sobre el estadio de su lesión de muñeca Alcaraz, que estuvo cinco meses sin poder competir, compartió que "no hay razón para golpear con miedo". "He estado entrenando con normalidad, golpeando la derecha con mucha libertad y sin pensar en la muñeca, ni durante los entrenamientos ni durante los partidos... Sé que, una vez que entro en la pista, tengo que ir a por todas en cada golpe. Tengo que sentirme normal y golpear como lo hacía antes de la lesión. Y después, veremos qué pasa. Ahora mismo me siento genial. No hay ninguna razón para tener miedo y no golpear con normalidad", aclaró el murciano.

articles.summary: Momentos de tensión en el US Open en la rueda de prensa de Aryna Sabalenka tras ganar a Polina Iatcenko
articles.body: Aryna Sabalenka cortó en seco las preguntas sobre su vida privada y actividades previas al US Open. La tenista bielorrusa tuvo un intercambio de palabras muy tenso e incómodo con un periodista en la rueda de prensa posterior a su triunfo por 6-1 y 6-1 ante Polina Iatcenko. Cuando el periodista trató de justificarse la tenista reaccionó molesta: "Ah, claro, antes no me tomaba las cosas en serio. Siguiente pregunta. Piensa antes de hablar".

articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz says he plans to take regular breaks from tennis in the future, even if that means skipping some tournaments. The Spaniard believes the packed ATP calendar is becoming too demanding and could leave players exhausted or injured.The defending US Open champion made the comments after fighting back from a first-set loss to beat Portugal’s Jaime Faria 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2 and reach the third round.Alcaraz recently returned after missing four months because of a wrist injury. While he did not want that long break, he now feels shorter, planned breaks could help him stay fresh.“I took more than I wanted, to be honest, but seeing how tight is the calendar, obviously I don’t want to have this break because an injury. But in the future, I’m going to take some breaks, some long breaks. Maybe not four months, but one month, two months, missing some tournaments, because it’s impossible to play them all,” Alcaraz said.Alcaraz concerned about player workloadThe 22-year-old feels players are being pushed to compete in too many major events, leaving little time to recover.“I think they adding more important tournaments. In a way they making us to play,” Alcaraz said. “You can decide your calendar, but there are some Masters 1000s, some Grand Slams, and we’ve been out playing 40 weeks if we got to play every mandatory tournament that the ATP required us to play,” he added.“So it’s impossible, and we are seeing a lot of players getting injured, a lot of players getting tired. If they don’t do anything about it, we are going to see even more in the future,” he warned.On court, Alcaraz recovered impressively after dropping the opening set. articles.title: The 2026 US Open is Killing the Ace
articles.summary: Through 44 completed men's singles matches at this year's US Open, covering 10,051 points, servers have produced 874 aces. That works out to an ace rate of 8...
articles.body:
Through 44 completed men's singles matches at this year's US Open , covering 10,051 points, servers have produced 874 aces. That works out to an ace rate of 8.7%, and if that number holds across the remaining matches, it would represent the lowest ace rate at any hard-court Grand Slam since the 2012 Australian Open, where the equivalent figure was 8.1%. For a tournament that has historically sat comfortably above 10%, and for a surface that is supposed to reward the big server more than any other, that number is worth examining.

The conditions at Flushing Meadows this year are doing something genuinely unusual to the serve, and several factors are pulling in different directions at once.

The Wilson Extra Duty ball used at the US Open is already a different animal from what players encounter at the other majors. It is slightly heavier than the ball used in the women's draw, fractionally different from the Dunlop ball used at Wimbledon, and built with a tighter felt weave than a standard Slazenger or Babolat. What makes it unpredictable is how it responds to the specific environmental conditions of the US Open.

New York in late summer is humid, oppressively humid. That humidity interacts with the ball, and it's felt in a way that matters enormously for servers. The humidity makes the ball's surface fluff up and expand faster, causing it to get dragged down during play. A coach at St. John's University, whose team trains in Flushing, explained it well: the ball gets heavier, so it doesn't move as fast. It gets fluffier. Wear and tear comes faster in humid heat than in dry heat.

The physics behind this are worth understanding, because they run counter to what most people assume about humidity and ball speed. Moist air is actually less dense than dry air, so in theory the ball meets less resistance in flight. But that is almost irrelevant next to what happens to the ball's felt. High humidity increases the felt's moisture content, adding mass. A heavier ball lands shorter and sits up. The air density effect, in other words, is a rounding error. The ball effect is the one players feel through their racket, and it is the one that suppresses aces.

The Day-to-Night Shift Makes It Stranger

What complicates the picture further is that conditions at the US Open aren't consistent across the tournament's sessions. Daytime matches and night sessions on Arthur Ashe Stadium play out in what amount to two different physical environments, and the effect on serving is not what casual intuition would suggest.

During the day, the heat is the dominant variable. Every 10°C rise costs about 1.1 percentage points off the first-serve-in rate and adds about 0.4 to the double-fault rate. Hotter conditions make the toss harder to control, make the grip sweatier, and increase the physical cost of generating racket head speed consistently over long matches. A serve that lands in the box cleanly in the first set becomes incrementally harder to repeat in the fourth.

At night, the dynamic shifts. Arthur Ashe Stadium seals itself rather than cools when the roof closes, running HVAC systems that provide cooling, air movement, and humidity control. The humidity trapped inside the bowl gets into the ball's felt and adds mass, which as already established favours the returner. Tennis Abstract's rolling surface speed ratings put the US Open at 0.99, just below tour average, with a 10.7% opponent-adjusted ace rate, against 1.11 and 11.9% at the Australian Open and 1.12 and 12.1% at Wimbledon.

That last figure is what provides context for the 8.7% currently being recorded. The US Open is already a below-average Slam for aces under normal conditions. When conditions are not normal, when humidity is elevated, and the felt is picking up moisture faster than usual, the number can drop significantly below even the historical baseline for this tournament.

The Court and Ball Combination This Year

Reports from Flushing Meadows this fortnight describe a surface that is notably faster than Cincinnati's courts were a week ago. Cincinnati registered a Court Pace Index of just 38.1 this year, significantly slower than its 2025 reading of 43, placing it roughly on par with Miami and below Indian Wells. By comparison, the Laykold surface at Flushing plays at a meaningfully higher pace, which would ordinarily translate to more aces, not fewer.

The paradox is in the ball. When the surface is fast, but the ball is heavy from humidity, you don't get a clean serving environment. You get a court that generates a low, skidding bounce that is genuinely difficult to return when the ball is traveling cleanly, combined with a ball that is resisting the server's attempt to generate pace. It sits awkwardly between two conditions, fast enough to reward aggressive play in rallies but heavy enough to reduce the explosive, flat, pure-pace serve that produces the category of ace most reliably.

The balls play lighter and more responsive at the start of a fresh can. Still, under New York humidity they deteriorate faster than at the Australian Open or Wimbledon, where conditions are either drier or more temperate.

What the number actually means is simple. The 8.7% figure, if it holds, would sit nearly two full percentage points below the US Open's recent historical average and more than two points below what Wimbledon and the Australian Open typically produce. That is a meaningful departure.

For the men still in the draw, the implications are real. Players who rely heavily on the free point from the serve, who have built their game around serving opponents off the court rather than engaging in extended baseline exchanges, will find the conditions less forgiving than the surface speed alone would suggest. The serve is less of a weapon when the ball misbehaves, which tilts the balance incrementally towards returners and players who are comfortable in longer rallies, in general towards the physical attrition style of tennis that the US Open in humid conditions tends to produce late in matches.

The 2012 Australian Open, the last hard-court Slam to record a lower ace rate than this one is currently tracking, was played in Melbourne's heat under its own distinctive conditions. That the 2026 US Open might match or challenge that benchmark, at a tournament built on big serving and fast hard courts, is one of the more extraordinary statistical stories of this fortnight.

Nobody is tracking it on the main scoreboards at the US Open. But it is happening, match by match, point by point, across a draw that is producing significantly fewer free points from serve than anyone walking into the tournament this year had reason to expect.

articles.title: Gael Monfils Might Be Old, But he is Never Dull
articles.summary: On September 1st 2026, Gael Monfils turned 40 years old. He also walked onto Louis Armstrong Stadium, won three consecutive sets after losing the first, hit...
articles.body:
On September 1st 2026, Gael Monfils turned 40 years old. He also walked onto Louis Armstrong Stadium, won three consecutive sets after losing the first, hit a leaping forehand winner at 1-0 in the fourth set, cupped his hand to his ear, and had the entire building giving him a standing ovation. There is no other player on the ATP Tour, active or retired, who could have manufactured that moment. There is no other player in the history of the sport who would have even tried.

This is what Monfils has always been, and what the sport will lose when he walks away at the end of this season. Not the greatest player of his generation, not a Grand Slam champion, not the player French tennis always hoped he might become. Something more complicated than any of that, and in its own way more irreplaceable. He is the greatest entertainer the game has ever produced. And on Tuesday night at Flushing Meadows, in his 18th and final appearance at a tournament he has loved for two decades, he reminded everyone why that title means something.

Gael Monfils def. Adolfo Daniel Vallejo 2-6 6-1 6-2 6-0

Adolfo Daniel Vallejo is 22 years old, ranked inside the world's Top 70, and arrived in New York as the No. 1 player from Paraguay having won five Challenger titles and reached the second round at Roland Garros earlier this year. He is not a name that sends fear through a draw, but he is a genuine professional who earned his spot in the main draw on merit. The match began in a manner that suggested Monfils was about to be politely ushered towards retirement. Vallejo took the first set 6-2 with relative ease.

Then Monfils did what Monfils has always done. He found the crowd, fed off it, and started playing tennis that had nothing to do with being 40. The second set went 6-1 to Monfils. The third went 6-2. When he broke to lead 1-0 in the fourth and then launched himself into the air to smash a forehand winner at a trajectory that had no business going in, spinning around to cup his hand to his ear afterwards, the match was not yet over but the occasion already was. He closed it out 6-0, firing 37 winners across the match and becoming the oldest player to win a main-draw singles match at Flushing Meadows since Jimmy Connors did exactly the same thing, on his own 40th birthday, in 1992.

It was his 34th career victory at the US Open, the most of any Frenchman in the tournament's history.

What He Was, and What He Could Have Been

The honest accounting of Monfils' career requires holding two things simultaneously. He was genuinely one of the most talented players of his generation, and he was also something less than that talent should have produced. He won his first junior Grand Slam at 17, eventually claiming three of the four Major boys' titles in a single year in 2004. He was voted ATP Newcomer of the Year in 2005. He reached the French Open semifinals in 2008, losing to Roger Federer, and the US Open semifinals in 2016, losing to Novak Djokovic. He finished 2016 ranked world No. 6, the highest of his career, and reached Masters 1000 finals in Paris twice and in Monte Carlo. He won 13 ATP titles across 20 seasons.

The career, viewed in the harsh light of statistics, was very good and fell short of great. Rafael Nadal, Federer and Djokovic consumed the Major titles throughout his prime years, which is a fact of life for virtually every player of his generation. But there was also a version of the conversation that suggested Monfils sometimes preferred the highlight to the victory and that the entertainent impulse which made him so magnetic could also dilute the competitive ruthlessness that separates good careers from transcendent ones. He missed 13 Grand Slam events across his career through injury.

What the statistics cannot capture, and what Elina Svitolina said well about her husband's legacy at Roland Garros earlier this year, is that statistics will never capture his whole unique greatness.

What New York Gave Him, and What He Gave Back

There is something magical about the relationship between Monfils and Flushing Meadows that goes beyond the results. New York has always been the right backdrop for him. The noise, the electricity, the crowds that stay late and respond to every point, the culture of the place that rewards audacity over restraint. He has shown up here eighteen times across twenty-one years, from 2005 to 2026, and the city has received him every single time like someone they were genuinely pleased to see. The 2016 semifinal run where he pushed Djokovic to four sets remains the peak result. But the highlight reel from across eighteen visits contains shots from every round of every year that players with three times the trophies could not produce.

This week he also partnered with Svitolina in the revamped mixed doubles event, the two of them reaching the semifinals together in the first time they had competed as a team. At some point during the fortnight his daughter Skai will see her father play professional tennis in the place he loves most, at the age of 40, still leaping off the ground to hit forehands at players half his age.

Monfils announced at the end of last year that this would be his final season. He will retire when the year ends, closing a career that stretched over more than two full decades and produced memories that sit outside the categories tennis uses to evaluate its players. He faces Learner Tien in the second round, an American wildly popular with the home crowd, and the outcome of that match is genuinely unpredictable, because outcomes involving Monfils have always been genuinely unpredictable.

But whether he wins or loses against Tien, Tuesday night at Louis Armstrong Stadium already happened. A 40-year-old man on his birthday, down a set against a player half his age came back to win 2-6 6-1 6-2 6-0 and had the crowd sung him happy birthday. Nobody planned it. Nobody scripted it. He just played tennis the only way he has ever known how to play it, and the building responded the way buildings have always responded to Monfils.

When he does eventually walk off a professional court for the last time, what the sport will be missing is not his ranking or his titles. It will be the simple, irreplaceable fact that watching him play tennis was always worth showing up for. At forty years old, in New York, on his birthday, he proved that one more time.
